t.1.37.1: The Sūta said: Thus addressed, the fiery Śṛṅgin, filled with anger, on hearing that his father was bearing a dead creature, was consumed with burning wrath.
t.1.37.3: Dear son, King Parikṣit, while roaming about on a hunt, has today hung a dead snake upon your father's shoulder.
t.1.37.2: Looking at Kṛśa and speaking pleasant words, he asked: “How is it that my father is today the bearer of a dead creature?”
t.1.37.5: That king Parikṣit, son of Abhimanyu, having gone out hunting, pierced a deer with a feathered arrow and pursued it all alone.
t.1.37.4: What wrong was done by my father to that evil-souled king? Tell me truly, Kṛśa, and behold the power of my austerity!
t.1.37.6: And the king, wandering in that great forest, did not see the deer; but as soon as he saw your father, who was keeping silent, he questioned him.
t.1.37.8: But he, bound by his vow of silence, did not answer him at all; and the king, with the tip of his bow, placed a serpent upon his shoulder.
t.1.37.7: Afflicted by hunger, thirst and weariness, he asked your father, who stood there motionless as a post, again and again about the lost deer.
t.1.37.9: Śṛṅgin, your father there sits even now just as before, firm in his vow; and that king too has gone back to his own city, Gajāhvaya.
t.1.37.10: Having heard this, the son of the ṛṣi stood as though propping up the sky, his eyes reddened with rage, as if blazing with fury.
t.1.37.11: But he, possessed by anger, the splendid one, overpowered by the force of his fury, touched water and then cursed the king.
t.1.37.12: That sinful king who placed a dead snake on the shoulder of my aged father, who was moreover in such distress—
t.1.37.15: Having thus cursed the king, the enraged Śṛṅgī went to his father, who was seated in that pasture, bearing the dead serpent.
t.1.37.14: Seven nights from now he will lead to the abode of Yama this despiser of the twice-born, who brings disgrace upon the Kurus.
t.1.37.16: Śṛṅgī, beholding his father with the dead snake lying upon his shoulder, became filled with anger once more.
t.1.37.17: Out of grief he shed tears and said this to his father: "Father, having heard of this outrage done to you by that wicked-souled man..."
t.1.37.18: Provoked by King Parikṣit, I cursed that king out of anger, with a fierce curse such as he, the vilest of the Kuru line, truly deserves.
t.1.37.19: On the seventh day Takṣaka, the foremost of serpents, will lead that sinner to the most dreadful abode of Vaivasvata.
t.1.37.21: We dwell in the realm of that lord of men, and we are protected by him in accordance with what is right; I do not approve of harm being done to him.
t.1.37.20: O brahman, to him who was thus filled with anger his father said: “You have not done what is pleasing to me, my son; this is not the dharma of ascetics.”
t.1.37.22: A king, however he may conduct himself, must always be forgiven by people like us, my son; for dharma, when it is violated, destroys in turn, there is no doubt.
t.1.37.25: But Parikṣit protects us especially well, just as his great-grandfather did, and just as subjects ought to be protected by a king.
t.1.37.24: Protected by kings whose vision is guided by the śāstras, dear son, we practise abundant dharma, and by right they have a share in it.
t.1.37.23: If the king did not protect us, great affliction would surely befall us; we would not be able to practise dharma as we please, my son.
t.1.37.27: Therefore this evil deed was done by you rashly, out of childishness, for the king in no way deserves a curse from us, my son.
t.1.37.13: Takṣaka, the foremost of serpents, a venomous snake of fierce fiery energy, exceedingly enraged and driven by the force of my words, shall burn that wicked one.
t.1.37.26: Without doubt, this was done here today by that poor man, hungry and weary, who did not know of this vow.
